All the fathers of the four families of wrathful kings possess wings of method and wisdom marked by vajras and so forth at the tips. They are adorned with the symbolic implements of their families and cemetery attire. They are beautiful with bone and jewel ornaments. The mothers are also adorned with bone and jewel ornaments. The wrathful kings of the four families are clearly generated in the mandala. Outside that, from the six lotus petals, the assembly of peaceful deities is generated in succession. From the east of the six petals, the deities are arranged: blue Samantabhadra holds a vajra and bell. Embracing Dharmadhatvi.

The Muni of the Hungry Ghosts is red, holding a casket. The Muni of the Hell-beings is black, holding fire and water. Outside that, on the lotus petals, the Bodhisattvas and Consorts are generated in succession from the east: white Kshitigarbha embraces white Lasya. Symbolic implements are a lotus, bell, and mirror. White Maitreya embraces pale white Pushpa. Symbolic implements are a Naga-tree, bell, and flower. Red Samantabhadra embraces blue Aloka. Symbolic implements are a stalk of grain, bell, and garland. ### ON THE HAṬHA YOGA PRADĪPIKĀ

**Root Text:**
**For the yogi whose awareness of the Power <note>the Kuṇḍalinī</note> has arisen, and who has abandoned all actions without exception, the Natural State <term>Sahajāvasthā</term> arises spontaneously. (11)**
**When the breath <term>prāṇa</term> flows through the Suṣumṇā and the mind enters the Void, then the knower of Yoga uproots all karmas. (12)**

->|| COMMENTARY ||<-

[Continuing from the previous verse:] When sleep occurs, the breath—the air—dissolves into the Void, the "Opening of Brahman" <term>Brahmarandhra</term>; it reaches a state of dissolution. The dissolution of the breath is simply the absence of its activity. (10)

**Regarding Verse 11 ("For the yogi whose awareness..."):** "Arisen" means born. The "awareness of the Power" refers to the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī. For that yogi by whom all actions—the entirety of them—have been abandoned or discarded. By means of physical posture <term>āsana</term>, physical activities are abandoned, yet activity remains in the breath and the senses. When mental activities are abandoned through withdrawal <term>pratyāhāra</term>, concentration <term>dhāraṇā</term>, meditation <term>dhyāna</term>, and cognitive absorption <term>samprajñāta-samādhi</term>, activity still remains in the intellect <term>buddhi</term>. This is because the pure Self <term>puruṣa</term> is unchanging and "is indeed unattached" <note>original Sanskrit: *asaṅgo hyayaṃ puruṣaḥ*, a famous Upanishadic quote</note>, whereas the intellect, which is composed of the quality of purity <term>sattvaguṇa</term>, is subject to change. (11)

Through highest dispassion <term>paravairāgya</term> or through the long-term practice of cognitive absorption <term>samprajñāta-samādhi</term>, once the activities of the intellect are abandoned, one remains in a state of unchanging self-nature. That itself is the Natural State <term>Sahajāvasthā</term>, the Fourth State <term>Turyāvasthā</term>, and Liberation While Living <term>Jīvanmukti</term>. It manifests spontaneously, without any further effort. This is supported by the scripture: "By that which you renounce, renounce that as well; one should become unattached through wisdom." <note>This suggests a total letting go, even of the tool of renunciation itself.</note> **Regarding Verse 12 ("When the breath..."):** When the breath—the air—is flowing in the Suṣumṇā, the middle channel...

->|| VERNACULAR EXPLANATION ||<-

Through various types of Great Seals <term>mahāmudrā</term> and other practices, when the Great Power—the Kuṇḍalinī—is awakened, the breath then dissolves into the Void of the "Opening of Brahman" <term>Brahmarandhra</term>. (10)

**Regarding Verse 11:** For the yogi in whom the awareness of the Kuṇḍalinī has arisen and who has removed all karmas: through the practice of posture <term>āsana</term>, the activities of the body are removed. However, activity still resides in the breath and senses. Through withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and cognitive absorption, the activities of the mind are removed. At that point, activity remains only in the intellect, and the intellect becomes pure <term>sattvic</term>. Through dispassion and the long practice of absorption, the activities of the intellect are also removed. Then, one is established in the unchanging self-nature. This is called the Natural State <term>Sahajāvasthā</term>. This is also called the Fourth State <term>Turyāvasthā</term>. In this state, the yogi attains Liberation While Living <term>Jīvanmukti</term> spontaneously, without needing to make further effort. (11)

**Regarding Verse 12:** And when the breath begins to move in the Suṣumṇā, which is the middle channel, then the internal faculty <term>antaḥkaraṇa</term> enters the Void of Brahman. At that time, the knower of yoga uproots all those karmas that were destined to be experienced <term>prārabdha karma</term>. (12)

<summary>This page describes how the awakening of the Kuṇḍalinī leads a yogi from physical and mental stillness to the "Natural State" (Sahajāvasthā), where effort ceases and all past karmas are destroyed. It explains the hierarchy of stillness, moving from the body to the senses, then the mind, and finally the intellect.</summary>

### Chapter XXI.

Others, indeed, by combining hard bodies with hard ones and soft with soft due to their natural affinity <note>original: "convenientiam"; a philosophical concept suggesting that like substances should naturally combine or act upon one another</note>, wished for these bodies to be transmuted by one another and to effect transmutation. Yet they were unable to achieve this because of their own lack of skill. For instance, when mixing the Sun <note>Gold</note> or the Moon <note>Silver</note> with Venus <note>Copper</note> or any other of the metals, they did not see those metals transformed into the Sun or the Moon by a firm and true transmutation. Instead, it inevitably happens that through the intense action <note>original: "expressione forti"</note> of fire, each of those imperfect bodies is separated from the mixture and burned away, while the perfect body remains or returns to its former nature.
